title: Success, failure and difficulty
subtitle: achieve, fulfil, backfire, cope with
summary: Learn the verbs of succeeding and the nouns they go with, the vocabulary of failure and difficulty, and the word families built on succeed, achieve and fulfil.

lesson.heading: Succeeding
lesson.text: **Succeed** is followed by *in* + -ing. **Manage** is followed by *to* + infinitive, and unlike succeed it can take a direct object. **Achieve** and **accomplish** both go with quantity phrases such as *a lot* and *a great deal*.

examples.text: We **succeeded in** persuading a lot of people to join our protest.
I **managed to** contact him just before he left his office.
I don't think I can **manage** the whole walk. I think I'll turn back.
We've **achieved / accomplished** a great deal in the last year.
Do you think his plan will **come off**?

lesson.heading: Which verb goes with which noun?
lesson.note: Achieve is more common than accomplish with nouns expressing goals and ambitions: The company has achieved all its goals/aims/targets for this year.

lesson.heading: Failing
rows: close down through lack of success (go under is informal)
have ups and downs, even if it finally succeeds
lesson.note: Plans and projects sometimes backfire. Companies often fold through lack of success. All your hard work may come to nothing.

lesson.heading: Difficulty
lesson.text: Note the patterns: **have difficulty (in) doing**, **find it difficult to do**, **have trouble doing** and **have bother with**. *Trouble* and *bother* are more informal.

examples.text: I have great **difficulty** getting up in the morning.
I **find it difficult to** remember the names of everybody in the class.
It's **hard/difficult to** hear what she's saying.
I often **have trouble** starting the car on cold mornings.
We've had a lot of **bother** with the neighbours lately.

lesson.heading: Coping
lesson.text: To **cope with** something is to deal successfully with a difficult situation. You can also use **cope** on its own.

examples.text: Can you **cope with** three more students? They've just arrived.
I've got no money and my girlfriend's left me. I need help; I can't **cope** any more.
We'll have to get an au pair. I just can't **cope**.

lesson.heading: Word formation
lesson.note: Difficult has no adverb: we say we did it with difficulty. The adverb from successful is successfully.

lesson.text: Difficulty and success are uncountable in these phrases: *great difficulty finding somewhere to live* (not ~~difficulties~~) and *considerable success with his first novel* (not ~~successes~~).

exercises.prompt: The management have ___ a no-strike agreement with the union.
exercises.explanation: You reach or secure an agreement.

exercises.prompt: Now I've ___ all my family responsibilities, I can retire and travel the world.
exercises.explanation: You fulfil an obligation or a responsibility.

exercises.prompt: The school building fund has failed to ___ its target of 250,000 pounds.
exercises.explanation: A target can be reached, attained or achieved.

exercises.prompt: Very few people ___ all their hopes and dreams in life.
exercises.explanation: You realise or fulfil a dream; you reach or secure an agreement.

exercises.prompt: I'm afraid that little plan of mine didn't ___ off.
exercises.explanation: To come off means to succeed; it is informal.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb with its noun.

exercises.statement: 'She succeeded to rise to the top of her profession' is correct English.
exercises.explanation: Succeed takes in + -ing: She succeeded in rising to the top of her profession.

exercises.statement: 'Do you ever have any trouble using this photocopier?' is correct English.
exercises.explanation: Correct - have trouble is followed by the -ing form, with no preposition.

exercises.statement: 'I'm amazed that you can cope all the work they give you' is correct English.
exercises.explanation: Cope takes with: I'm amazed that you can cope with all the work they give you.

exercises.statement: 'Did you have many difficulties finding the book in the library?' is the preferred form.
exercises.explanation: Difficulty is uncountable here: Did you have much difficulty finding the book in the library?

options: I find it very difficult to understand English idioms.
I find very difficult to understand English idioms.
I find it very difficulty to understand English idioms.
I find very difficultly to understand English idioms.
exercises.explanation: The pattern is find it difficult to do something - the it is essential.

exercises.prompt: Unfortunately, it seems as if all Johnny's plans have come ___ nothing.
exercises.explanation: The fixed phrase is come to nothing.

exercises.prompt: Does the expression describe success or failure?
